extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, and publishers using the Chicago Manual of Style
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and conventions from the University of Chicago Manual of Style covering capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation for preparing manuscripts and printed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of administrative bodies and official units
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitals for names of institutions, schools, divisions, departments, boards, senates, councils, faculties, official offices and formal titles; e.g., the University, the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology, the Board of Trustees, the President, the Registrar, Professor of Physics, Van Husen Scholarship, courses in Political Economy, Autumn Quarter, First Term, Hall (for dormitories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal institutional names and official designations as proper nouns; provide examples and preferred short forms in parentheses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date line, salutatory, and signature formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Capitals and Small Capitals for the names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set date line to the right with an em indent in smaller type if desired. Examples: 'Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1910' (centered or right-set); salutatory set flush followed by a colon: 'My dear Mr. Smith:'; signature lines set to the right: 'Charles W. Scott'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize wording introducing resolutions/notes/sections
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes), use 'Note.' followed by period and dash; in constitutions and by-laws use 'Section' to introduce paragraphs and follow it by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate 'Section' after the first occurrence (e.g., 'Section 1. ...' then 'Sec. 2. ...'). Example: 'Note. — It should be noticed that ...' and 'Section 1. This association shall be styled ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small capitals for certain abbreviations (A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M. (ante/post meridiem), and B.C. and A.D. in small capitals and without a space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '11:30 A.M.'; '53 B.C., 1906 A.D.' (see related rules for time/date formatting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lowercase initial for commonized proper names and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage originally proper names, and their derivatives, and generally verbs derived from proper names, take a small (lower-case) initial when the origin is obscure or the term is generalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, boycott, roman (type), italicize, christianize.' See cross-references for related capitalization rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercase/minor-subdivision abbreviations in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor subdivisions and their abbreviations (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note) should be lowercased and abbreviated where appropriate: 'chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rules (37, 110, 236) for full bibliographic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate common units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use abbreviated forms for units of measure in many contexts: 'h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd. = yard; ft. = foot; etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow context conventions (textual vs. technical) and cross-reference typographic rules (see 111 for metric system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic side-heads: capitalize only first word and proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, set all but the first word and proper names in small (lower-case) initial letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for more on heads and subheads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercase first word of a connected quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a quotation is immediately connected with the preceding text (through a conjunction or otherwise), lower-case the initial word of the quotation even if it begins a sentence in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to lend emphasis, importance, or distinction in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case.'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life ...' Use emphasis sparingly and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize foreign words and short foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text and not yet incorporated into English should be italicized; also single sentences or brief passages in a foreign language not long enough to be set in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'Napoleon's coup d'état', 'Z>c gustibus non est disputandum.' Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or foreign institution/place names commonly used in English (see next rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize certain foreign names/places that are anglicized or institutional titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names, or names of foreign institutions or places whose meaning or position in English requires roman type or which are used in English as-is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Père Lagrange, Freiherr von Schwenau; the German Reichstag, the Champs Elysées, the Museo delle Terme.' Also do not italicize widely anglicized words (a posteriori, entree, per cent, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize titles of books and periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of publications—books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, and single long poems), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals—should be set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Independent, the Modern Language Review, the Chicago Tribune.' Note exceptions (e.g., Botanical Gazette practice) and that books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts are printed in roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts in roman
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of the Bible (canonical and apocryphal) and titles of ancient manuscripts should be set in roman (not italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references (31 and 44) for related typographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize certain Latin/technical abbreviations, but not others
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary and legal references, use italics for words/abbreviations like 'ibid., idem, loc. cit., op. cit., ad loc., s.v., supra, infra, passim, vide, circa (ca.)' but do not italicize 'cf., i.e., e.g., V. (versus), viz., etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow context: bibliographic/legal usages typically italicize classical Latin citations; common abbreviations used as part of English text remain roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set 'See' and 'See also' distinctively in indices
rubrics_metrics.description: In an index or similar compilation, set the words 'See' and 'See also' in a differentiated style (the Manual notes this usage under italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic differentiation where desirable for clarity in cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting of legal citations: names of parties and special prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: In citation of legal causes, set the names of plaintiff and defendant, and titles of proceedings containing prefixes like 'In re', 'Ex parte', and 'In the matter of' according to the style (noted under italics and quotation rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Connolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.' Follow typographic standards used in the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address lines and primary address formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters should be set flush on a separate line, with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:'; 'Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.'; 'Dear Sir: I take pleasure in announcing ...' (See rule 64.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and formatting of signatures and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name follows layout rules: one-word titles run into the same line; longer titles center under the name and indent as necessary according to length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' (one-line); 'Carter H. Harrison\nMayor of Chicago' (multi-line placement subject to special cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parenthetical letters for subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph; double parentheses if run in); use a, b, c affixed to numbers to denote fractional parts (e.g., Luke 4:31a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow consistent parenthesis conventions when enumerating or indicating fractional verse/page parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize letters used for algebraic/geometric quantities and for references to letters in diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters used to designate unknown quantities, lines, powers, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter (and letters referring to corresponding letters in illustrations) are set in italic type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ac + bc = c(a + b)'; 'At the point A above (see diagram).'; 'the nth power.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Set references to particular letters in roman/italic as typographic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: References to particular letters (e.g., 'the letter u, a small v') should be typographically distinguished (the Manual places these under the italics rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate type style for single-letter references consistent with mathematical and linguistic convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shillings and pence abbreviations following numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 's.' and 'd.' (= shillings and pence) following numerals where applicable: e.g., '3s. 6d.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow historic/numismatic style conventions in texts dealing with old currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize scientific (Latin) names of genera and species
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, botanical, and geological matter, scientific Latin names of genera and species when used together should be printed in italics; in astronomical matter, constellations and star names are italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Saturn, Cassiopeia.' Note: in medical matter the practice is often to print such names in roman (avoid italics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions set the introductory word 'Resolved' (See rule 39) according to the typographic conventions described in the manual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow resolution formatting conventions consistent with capitalization and layout elsewhere in the style guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Continued'/'To be continued' after headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, indicate continuation with the word 'Continued' or 'To be continued' at the end of articles when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example formatting: 'THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY— Continued' or bracketed note '[To be continued]'. See rule 179 for continuation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for inline citations (roman-quote)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words should be put between quotation marks (roman type for the quoted matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 74 and cross-reference rules for longer extracts that may be set in smaller type instead of run-in quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for consecutive quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors, or from different works by the same author, following each other uninterrupted by original matter or references should each be enclosed in quotation marks even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 75; when multiple quoted passages follow without intervening original text, apply quotation marks to each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for definitions, unusual words, translations, and attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for (a) a word or phrase accompanied by its definition; (b) unusual, technical, or ironical words or phrases; (c) English equivalents in translations; and (d) particular words or phrases to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '"Drop-folio" means a page-number at the foot of the page.'; 'Her "five o'clocks" were famous.'; 'Weltanschauung, "world-view" ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks for serial titles, short poems, papers, and shorter subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Set serial series titles, titles of shorter poems, and cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters), papers, lectures, sermons, toasts, mottoes, etc., in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.'; 'English Men of Letters' series; 'The Introduction contains ...' (preface/index references may be capitalized without quotation marks per note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of ships and works of art in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of ships and titles of works of art should be set in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon'; Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Set long quotations in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, all prose extracts that will make five or more lines in the smaller type, and all poetry citations of two lines or more, should be set in smaller (reduced) type rather than run into the body text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated prose quotation may be run in if it bears an organic relation to the argument. Where passages are set in smaller type, reduce font sizes accordingly (see rule 86 for size reductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced citations generally omit quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations set in smaller type should not have quotation marks, except in the cases noted (e.g., consecutive quoted authors per rule 75); likewise avoid quotation marks with italics in reduced citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 85–87 for details on when to reduce type and how to format reduced citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when they represent omitted matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses, and the phrase 'etc.' when it otherwise would not be clear that it stands for an omitted part of the quoted matter; clarity in each case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in rule 88 illustrate when 'etc.' belongs inside or outside quotation marks depending on whether it stands for omitted text of the quotation or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat opening quotation marks for each paragraph of a multi-paragraph quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted prose matter broken into paragraphs should have the opening quotation marks repeated at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aids the reader in seeing that the quotation continues across paragraphs (see rule 89).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearing quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment of a block quotation is desired, the quotation marks should be 'cleared'—i.e., projected beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates opening quotation mark projecting beyond left-alignment for visual consistency (rule 90).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use double quotes for primary quotations and alternate single/double for nested quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation use single marks; alternate back to double for a third-level quotation and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in rule 91 shows nesting: double → single → double → single as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out most civil and military titles before names; abbreviate certain honorifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out civil and military titles and forms of address (preceding the name) in full except for Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon. (these are abbreviated); Esq. following the name should be abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: in quotations or original signatures the abbreviated forms may appear. Do not set 'the Rev.' or 'the Hon.' except in quotations. See rule 92.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out Christian (given) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use full Christian/given names (e.g., George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviations like Geo., Chas., Jno., except where the abbreviated form is in quoted matter or original signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 93 and cross-references for name-part capitalization (239).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers under three digits in ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless of statistical/technical character or occurring in long groups; treat all numbers in connected groups alike and use figures if the largest contains three or more digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities ...' but 'He spent 128 days ...'. Use 'per cent' in figures. See rule 94 for many examples and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out round (approximate) numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Round/approximate figures (e.g., 'about five hundred') are spelled out; however exact figures should be given in numerals when appropriate (exceptions e.g., 550).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but 'at 550'); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but 'about 2,700'). See rule 95.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers that begin a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, no matter how large, that commence a sentence in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When impracticable, rephrase to avoid beginning a sentence with a numeral. Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, and 126 children ...' (rule 96).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out isolated sums of money in ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out (e.g., 'The admission was two dollars').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When several such numbers occur close together or in statistical matter, use figures and currency symbols: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.' (rule 97).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of day formatting in prose and technical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day in ordinary reading-matter: spell out ('at four', 'at half-past two in the afternoon'); in statistical/enumerative contexts or when paired with A.M./P.M. use figures (e.g., 'at 4:15 P.M.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'o'clock' in statistical contexts. See rule 98.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out ages in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Ages are normally spelled out in prose: 'eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerals where technical/statistical style dictates differently. See rule 99.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out names of centuries and comparable historical/political numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, and thoroughfares are spelled out (e.g., 'nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures only when brevity or context suggests (see rules 7, 8, 13). See rule 100.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to decades in words
rubrics_metrics.description: References to particular decades are styled in words (e.g., 'in the nineties').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 101 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of months spelled out except in certain contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out names of months in ordinary prose, but use figures/abbreviations in statistical matter or long enumerations (e.g., 'from January 1 to April 15').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit ordinal suffixes (st, nd, th) after dates. See rule 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full 'United States' in most prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'United States' spelled out in running text (except in quotations and certain technical connections; see footnote examples), and use abbreviations in footnotes/certain references as specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include military/publisher abbreviations like 'U.S. Geological Survey' and abbreviations for person/title contexts (see rule 103).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out 'Railroad(-way)', 'Fort', and 'Mount' in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out 'Railroad' (or 'Railway'), and use 'Fort' and 'Mount' in geographical appellations as words rather than abbreviations where applicable (e.g., 'Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad'; 'Fort Wayne', 'Mount Elias').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full words for clarity unless technical or stylistic reasons suggest otherwise (rule 104).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally spell out names of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out the full names of publications in running text unless context (technical/bibliographic) dictates abbreviated or contracted forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author preference guide exceptions; when in doubt, spell out (rule 105).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate state names following town names (specified set)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a state name follows a town in an address or date line, use standard abbreviated forms (no spaces between letters) such as 'Ala., Ariz., Cal., Conn., D.C., Ill., Mass., N.Y., Pa., etc.' as listed in rule 106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the manual's table of state abbreviations and use consistently with date-line and address formatting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use ampersand in technical bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies) abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use '&' for 'and' in firm names (e.g., 'Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In running text (non-technical) it is acceptable to spell out 'Company' and 'Brothers' for readability: 'Harper Brothers have recently published ...' (rule 107).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' in place names but omit before apostles/church fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' before many place names and churches (e.g., 'St. Louis, St. Peter's Church'), but preferably omit 'St.' when referring to apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (e.g., 'Luke, Paul, Augustine' rather than 'St. Luke').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow tradition and clarity; see rule 108 for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard abbreviations for books of the Bible in references
rubrics_metrics.description: In references to Scripture passages use prescribed abbreviations for books of the Old Testament, New Testament, and Apocrypha (e.g., 'Gen., Exod., Matt., John, Rev., Wisd. of Sol., Sus., Tob.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the manual's complete lists in rule 109 for the accepted abbreviations and forms to use in bibliographic and footnote contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate bibliographic units (Vol., No., chap., art., sec., p., col., vs., n.)
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references and bibliographic contexts abbreviate units like volume, number, chapter, article, section, page, column, verse, and note when followed by their numbers (e.g., 'Vol. I, No. 1, chap. ii, art. iii, sec. 4, p. 5, col. 6, vs. 7').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the manual's conventions for pluralization and page-range notation (see rule 110).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate metric and common measurement symbols after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metric unit abbreviations and common measurement symbols when following numerals: '1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. (= cubic meter), c.c., gm. (= gram), gr. (=grain), h. (=hour), min. (=minute), sec. (=second), lb., oz., yd., ft., in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow context-sensitive typographic spacing conventions; see rule 111 for examples and cross-references to special journal practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow original spelling/punctuation for Old English quotations; use office style otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ only slightly, apply Office style; in citations from Old English works or where faithfulness to the original is essential, follow the original copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always accurately quote titles; use editorial judgment about modernization vs. fidelity (rule 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form possessives of proper names ending in s or sibilants by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: For monosyllabic proper names ending in s or another sibilant, form the possessive by adding apostrophe + s (e.g., 'Marx's theories'); for names of more than one syllable ending in sibilant, add an apostrophe alone (e.g., 'Moses' law', 'Jesus' birth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow convention for clarity and ease of pronunciation; see rule 113 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'a' before sounded A, long u, and the word 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a sounded A, a long u, and the word 'one' use 'a' (e.g., 'a hotel', 'a union', 'a euphonious word', 'such a one').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the preferred indefinite-article form in formal prose (rule 114).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use Latin ligatures in quotations from Latin; use ligatures in certain modern languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using ligatures (æ, œ) separated as 'ae' or 'oe' in Latin quotations and anglicized derivatives where appropriate; however, in quotations from Old English, French and other modern languages it is incorrect to separate such letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Aurea prima ...' vs. 'Œuvres de Balzac, chef-d'œuvre.' (rule 115).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' for physical distance or 'more remote' and 'further' for 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.' (rule 116).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'O' (without comma) for vocatives; use 'Oh,' with comma for exclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use the single-letter 'O' without a comma following; for an exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?' (rule 117).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles retaining or omitting final -e
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' (agreeing, dyeing, hoeing, eyeing, shoeing, singeing, tingeing, vieing); others omit the final e before 'r' (acknowledging, grudging, trudging, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the manual's list (rule 118) for standardized participle spellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the Manual's prescribed spelling list and one-word conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the Manual's standard spellings for a long list of words (e.g., 'abridgment, acknowledgment, canceled, color, center, theater, neighbor, rumor, traveler, etc.') and make one word of compounds like 'anyone, someone, today, tomorrow, tonight, cannot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the comprehensive list in rule 119 and note the Manual's stance on -ise vs -ize endings in rule 120.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate -ise and -ize spellings according to prescribed lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '-ise' for verbs like 'advertise, advise, comprise, exercise' and '-ize' (or '-yze') for verbs like 'aggrandize, analyze, authorize, emphasize', following the Manual's two-column lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the provided word lists (rule 120) to determine the preferred termination for each verb; note instances where both senses/meanings produce different words (e.g., 'appraise' vs 'apprize').

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation font/face matches preceding word
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: punctuation following italicized words uses italic punctuation. See rule 121.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use period to end complete sentences and after most abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence and is put after abbreviations except where mechanical necessity or technical convention excludes it (e.g., some metric symbols, chemical symbols, certain journal abbreviations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, No. 1, Chas.'; but not '2 per cent' or 'Fe' (chemical symbols). See rule 122–123 for exceptions and journal-specific practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period after Roman numerals even when they have the value of ordinals (e.g., 'Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 124.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running heads, centered headlines, and non-sentence legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place a period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions, legends that are not complete sentences, date lines, or signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves clean typographic appearance for headings and labels (rule 125).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place period inside quotation marks; parentheses placement depends on independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods go inside closing quotation marks. Place periods inside parentheses if the matter enclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise place them outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an inviolable rule in the Manual: 'Tennyson's
